name: Governance
blurb: Audit frameworks, accountability structures, and the evidence on which audits change anything.

papers.note: The founding internal audit framework, and the source of the document per stage audit report structure now common in practice.
papers.title: Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency

papers.note: Breaks accountability into seven features and four goals, giving precise language for a governance charter.
papers.title: Accountability in artificial intelligence: what it is and how it works

papers.note: Synthesises technical, legal, ethical and multi stakeholder approaches into one transparency and accountability review.
papers.title: Transparency and accountability in AI systems: safeguarding wellbeing in the age of algorithmic decision-making

papers.note: Sets out the three AAA principles of risk assessment, audit trails and jurisdictional adherence for independent audit.
papers.title: Governing AI safety through independent audits

papers.note: Argues that the shortage of technical capability inside regulators, not the absence of will, is what produced regulatory inertia, and that the borderless nature of the problem demands coordination no single jurisdiction can supply.
papers.title: AI Governance in a Complex and Rapidly Changing Regulatory Landscape: A Global Perspective

papers.note: Sets out the governance problems specific to generative systems, from data provenance and intellectual property to concentration of power among a few firms, and argues for participatory rather than technocratic oversight.
papers.title: Governance of Generative AI

papers.note: Finds only a subset of AI audits produce accountability outcomes, and isolates what separates the effective ones.
papers.title: AI auditing: The Broken Bus on the Road to AI Accountability
papers.journal: IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning

papers.note: 35 practitioner interviews and 435 tools reviewed, the best available map of where audit tooling actually falls short.
papers.title: Towards AI Accountability Infrastructure: Gaps and Opportunities in AI Audit Tooling
papers.journal: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems

papers.note: Compares regulatory approaches across the United States, EU, Asia, Africa and the Americas, and proposes adaptive rules that can move at the pace of the technology rather than the pace of legislation.
papers.title: Managing the race to the moon: Global policy and governance in Artificial Intelligence regulation

papers.note: Survey evidence from 228 practitioners that IT governance is the mechanism through which AI adoption reaches audit quality.
papers.title: The Role of IT Governance in the Integration of AI in Accounting and Auditing Operations

papers.note: Points out that deep-learning systems cannot be audited against a specification the way aircraft can, then argues the expert-agency model still applies, with licensing, disclosure and rapid intervention.
papers.title: When code is not law: rethinking regulation for artificial intelligence

papers.note: Assesses United States governance strategy specifically, including the legal risks attaching to generated content, and proposes where a dedicated regulator would help.
papers.title: Balancing Innovation and Regulation in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence

papers.note: Models AI audit on financial audit practice and works the criteria through NYC Local Law 144 bias audits.
papers.title: A Framework for Assurance Audits of Algorithmic Systems
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency

papers.note: Analyses twelve African countries and finds usable governance capability already sitting in banking model management and electronic transactions law, rather than assuming a blank slate.
papers.title: Responsible artificial intelligence in Africa: towards policy learning

papers.note: A dissent from the consensus: argues risk classification underweights circular effects, the difficulty of measuring risk at all, and geopolitical power imbalance.
papers.title: Limitations of risk-based artificial intelligence regulation: a structuration theory approach

papers.note: Governance as code with signed evidence artifacts and clause level traceability across EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001.
papers.title: From Policy to Pipeline: A Governance Framework for AI Development and Operations Pipelines
